overview: Black answers 1.Nf3 with the flank move 1...a6, preparing ...b5, ...Bb7 and ...e6 as a hypermodern set-up and keeping options open. White can take the centre with e4 and d4 or fianchetto; Black reacts with ...b5, ...Bb7 and ...e6, or ...c5. It is an offbeat way to avoid theory; it costs a tempo and gives White easy development.

white_ideas.idea: Occupy the centre with e4 and d4 and develop with ease while Black's a-pawn move is slow.
Play c4 and g3 and keep a flexible English or Réti set-up.

black_ideas.idea: Fianchetto the queen's bishop with ...b5 and ...Bb7 and attack the centre from the wings.
Develop with ...e6, ...c5 and ...Nf6 and transpose to a Sicilian or Hedgehog-type game.

typical_structures.structure: Black queenside pawns on a6 and b5 with a bishop on b7 against a White centre.

character.notes: Slow and flexible; neither side is forced into tactics early.

gambit.notes: Just a pawn move, no material is given.

soundness.notes: Loses a tempo but Black is not worse by force.

structure.notes: The centre is undecided and the setup is flank-led.

approach.notes: Strong players seldom answer 1.Nf3 with 1...a6; it is a surprise weapon.

level.notes: Little theory and loose plans; not a beginner choice.

character.reason: Slow flexible play that is neither especially solid nor forcing.

soundness.reason: A wasted tempo but nothing is refuted.

structure.reason: The centre is left open to many set-ups.

approach.reason: Seldom played by strong players and chosen for surprise.

level.reason: Not a beginner choice and little theory.

plans.reason: Black aims for ...b5 and a bishop on b7.
